clue.text: Can a messenger be an asset to a greengrocer?

parts.note: a runner is someone who carries messages
these two words run together spell the second word of the answer

explanation.surface: A question whether a courier could be useful to a shopkeeper selling vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads straight through: a messenger (RUNNER) followed by the words 'be an' written as one word gives the vegetable a greengrocer sells.
explanation.definitionFit: This climbing legume is a staple vegetable stocked by a greengrocer, so it is one of his saleable goods.

clue.text: Stretch, leading to ruin

definitions.meaning: to stretch, as on the torture frame
the phrase '... and ruin' means total decay

explanation.surface: Overreaching that ends in disaster.
explanation.definitionFit: The torture frame pulled limbs taut, and 'rack and ruin' pairs the word with destruction.

clue.text: Saved by timely repair

parts.note: the proverb says a stitch in time saves this number

explanation.surface: Something rescued by fixing it promptly.
explanation.walkthrough: From 'a stitch in time saves nine': mending early avoids many more stitches later.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb names this number as the stitches saved by mending promptly.

clue.text: Ben put this man in his 11

definitions.text: Ben put this man in his 11

parts.words: Ben put this man in his 11
parts.note: Ben Jonson's comedy title runs '___ Man in His' followed by the answer to 11-down

explanation.surface: A man named Ben placed someone in his team of eleven.
explanation.walkthrough: '11' looks like a cricket or football eleven, but it points to 11-down: Ben Jonson's 1598 comedy is 'Every Man in His Humour'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word opens the title of Ben Jonson's comedy about men ruled by their temperaments.

clue.text: Typical business-man from Lewis

parts.note: Sinclair Lewis's 1922 novel portrays a conformist small-town American businessman, whose name became a byword

explanation.surface: A characteristic businessman from the Scottish isle of Lewis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lewis' suggests the Hebridean island, but it is the American novelist Sinclair Lewis, whose title character is a complacent realtor.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinclair Lewis's title character became a common noun for a smug, materialistic businessman.

clue.text: Stuffy-or bald, unlike Robin of the song ?

definitions.meaning: a stuffy room lacks fresh air

definitions.text: bald, unlike Robin of the song
definitions.meaning: dropping the H from hairless; the song is Robin Adair, and Adair sounds like 'a hair' with the H dropped

explanation.surface: A stuffy, bald man, compared with the hero of an old song.
explanation.walkthrough: Robin Adair is an old Irish ballad; said with a dropped H, 'Adair' is 'a hair', so Robin had one while a bald man is ''airless'.
explanation.definitionFit: A close room lacking ventilation, and, dropping the H, a head with no hair.

clue.text: Fitzgerald's original, isn't he:?.

parts.note: Edward FitzGerald's famous Victorian poem was a free translation of a Persian poet's quatrains, so that poet is his original

explanation.surface: A question about who inspired the work of a writer called Fitzgerald.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward FitzGerald published the Rubaiyat in 1859, an English version of verses by the Persian astronomer-poet Khayyam; the man behind the translation is his 'original'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Persian poet Khayyam wrote the quatrains that FitzGerald rendered into English, making him the source of that translation.

clue.text: Hunter's principal source of power

parts.note: a hunter is a pocket watch with a hinged cover, driven by a coiled spring

explanation.surface: What gives a huntsman his strength.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hunter' suggests a huntsman, but it is a hunter watch, whose movement is driven by its chief coiled spring.
explanation.definitionFit: The principal coiled spring in a watch drives its movement, and figuratively means the chief motive force.

clue.text: Just the outfit to smarten up: Rotten Row

parts.note: right means just or fair
a dress is an outfit of clothing

explanation.surface: Fine clothes to look smart on Rotten Row, the fashionable riding track in London's Hyde Park.
explanation.walkthrough: Rotten Row is a riding track in Hyde Park where society once paraded; here it is a ragged row of soldiers, ordered to line up straight.
explanation.definitionFit: This drill command makes soldiers align with the man on their right, straightening an untidy rank.

clue.text: It's a sort of bell see?

definitions.meaning: the ... bell is a garden campanula, a flower named after a city
a see is a bishop's diocese; this one is the seat of the senior English archbishop

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about a type of bell, as if asking someone to look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'see' looks like the verb 'look' with a question mark, but it is the church sense: the diocese of an archbishop.
explanation.definitionFit: The city names both a campanula flower and the archbishop's diocese, the premier see of the Church of England.

clue.text: By sharp practice they get a lot cheaper

definitions.text: By sharp practice they get a lot cheaper

parts.words: By sharp practice they get a lot cheaper
parts.note: dealers who agree not to bid against each other at auction buy each lot for less, then share out the goods privately

explanation.surface: Cheats who use dodgy methods to buy things at a discount.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lot' looks like 'a great deal', but it is an auction lot: a ring is an illegal cartel of dealers who keep auction prices down by not bidding against one another.
explanation.definitionFit: A dealers' ring is a group colluding at auctions so members can buy items cheaply and divide them afterwards.

clue.text: Indulge one of the senses

definitions.meaning: to go along with their wishes
a sense of fun and wit is one of the faculties people speak of having

explanation.surface: An invitation to treat one of the five senses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one of the senses' suggests sight or taste, but it is the sense of comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: To pander to someone's whims is one meaning, and a person's sense of comedy is the other.

clue.text: Acknowledgment of a reporter -and how he gets paid?

definitions.meaning: the printed credit line naming the journalist who wrote a newspaper story
read as two words: a freelance reporter was paid by the number of lines printed

explanation.surface: A remark about crediting a journalist and the method of paying him.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition splits the answer into 'by line', the old rate of payment for newspaper contributors per printed line.
explanation.definitionFit: A credit naming a story's writer appears atop the article, and reporters were once paid per printed line.

clue.text: Disturbed by auction price

definitions.meaning: ... as an adjective means troubled or agitated
the ... price is the lowest figure at which a seller will let an auction lot go, the reserve

explanation.surface: Someone troubled by the price something fetched at an auction.
explanation.definitionFit: Being agitated is the everyday sense, while in auctions the reserve figure is the traditional term for the starting price.

clue.text: He should not decrease, but enlarge one's public image

definitions.text: He should not decrease, but enlarge one's public image

parts.words: He should not decrease, but enlarge one's public image
parts.note: press can mean flatten, but this publicist's job is to build up a client's reputation in the newspapers

explanation.surface: Someone told to make a reputation bigger, not smaller.
explanation.walkthrough: Pressing flattens, so the first word suggests making smaller; this agent instead enlarges a client's image in the press.
explanation.definitionFit: A publicist employed to place favourable stories in newspapers and promote a client's reputation.

clue.text: "She is in her grave, and, oh, The, to me!" (Wordsworth)

definitions.text: "She is in her grave, and, oh, The, to me!" (Wordsworth)

parts.words: "She is in her grave, and, oh, The, to me!" (Wordsworth)
parts.note: the closing line of Wordsworth's Lucy poem 'She dwelt among the untrodden ways', with its key word missing

explanation.surface: A quotation from Wordsworth with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: The poem ends: 'But she is in her grave, and, oh, / The difference to me!'
explanation.definitionFit: Wordsworth's line mourns the change Lucy's death makes to the speaker, and this word fills the gap.

clue.text: Less than the body of the Gospel

definitions.text: Less than the body of the Gospel

parts.words: Less than the body of the Gospel
parts.note: in the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus asks whether the body is not more than the clothes it wears

explanation.surface: Something reckoned smaller than the main text of a book of the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'body of the Gospel' suggests the main text, but it is the human body: Matthew 6:25 says 'Is not the life more than meat, and the body than' this clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: This old word for clothing is what the Gospel says counts for less than the body that wears it.

clue.text: Paris star at the crossroads

definitions.meaning: the French word for a star
a star-shaped meeting of avenues, as at the Place Charles de Gaulle around the Arc de Triomphe

explanation.surface: A Parisian celebrity standing at a road junction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'star' suggests a celebrity, but it is the French word; the Paris square where twelve avenues meet is still called the Étoile.
explanation.definitionFit: French for star, and a junction of avenues radiating like a star's points.

clue.text: Sporting recorder interrupted by upstart cleaner

indicators.note: the scorekeeper's word is broken into, with the other piece placed in the gap

parts.note: a scorer records the points in a game
read as the start of 'up', its first letter U

explanation.surface: A games scorekeeper is cut short by an impudent newcomer who cleans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upstart' looks like a presumptuous person, but it is read as 'up' + 'start', the start of the word up, U.
explanation.definitionFit: A pad or person that scrubs pots clean is a scrubbing tool or agent of cleaning.

clue.text: Do they pull. their punches here? On the contrary

definitions.text: Do they pull. their punches here? On the contrary

parts.words: Do they pull. their punches here? On the contrary
parts.note: the county breeds heavy draught horses called punches, so here the punches pull rather than being pulled

explanation.surface: A question about boxers holding back, answered with a reversal.
explanation.walkthrough: Boxing's 'pull their punches' is turned round: the Suffolk Punch is an English heavy cart horse, so in this county the punches do the pulling. Suffolk is a county in eastern England.
explanation.definitionFit: The eastern English county gave its name to the Punch breed of draught horse that hauls carts and ploughs.

clue.text: One tends to be blue, in the vicinity of this joint

definitions.text: One tends to be blue, in the vicinity of this joint

parts.words: One tends to be blue, in the vicinity of this joint
parts.note: a risque joke is said to be near this finger joint, and blue means risque

explanation.surface: Someone who feels sad when near a pub or nightclub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blue' suggests sad and 'joint' a bar, but the idiom is 'near the knuckle', meaning bordering on the indecent.
explanation.definitionFit: A finger joint, and the idiom placing indecent humour 'near' it.

clue.text: Take income from bachelor flats to sea

parts.note: BA, Bachelor of Arts, the graduate degree, stands for a bachelor
a landlord rents flats out, taking money from them

explanation.surface: An instruction to collect rent from single men's apartments and go off to sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The flats are what the landlord rents; put BA (a Bachelor of Arts) in front to name an Arctic sea north of Norway and Russia.
explanation.definitionFit: This Arctic body of water north of Scandinavia and Russia is named after the Dutch navigator Willem Barentsz.

clue.text: It's hardly sensible to seek inspiration in bed

indicators.note: one piece lies inside the bed, as a sleeper lies in one

parts.note: taken as written
to muse is to ponder, seeking ideas

explanation.surface: Lying in bed waiting for ideas is not a sensible plan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in bed' looks like part of the picture of a lazy writer, but 'in' is the container signal; the classical Muse as goddess of inspiration gives the surface its sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone bewildered and confused is far from clear-headed.

clue.text: Day of uncertain glory

parts.note: Shakespeare's Two Gentlemen of Verona speaks of love resembling the uncertain glory of a spring day of this month

explanation.surface: A day whose splendour may not last.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is from The Two Gentlemen of Verona: 'The uncertain glory of an April day', changeable spring weather.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's line attaches fickle brightness to a day in this showery spring month.

clue.text: Like the born poet, whose bed is so untidy

definitions.meaning: the proverb says poets are born, not made, so a born poet was never made
a bed left without its covers straightened has not been made

explanation.surface: A natural-born poet with a messy bedroom.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'poets are born, not made' (Latin poeta nascitur, non fit) gives the first sense; the second is a bed nobody has tidied.
explanation.definitionFit: A natural poet was not manufactured by training, and an untidy bed has not been straightened.

clue.text: He dated many of his pictures A.D.

definitions.text: He dated many of his pictures A.D.

parts.words: He dated many of his pictures A.D.
parts.note: the German artist marked his prints with a monogram of his initials, A over D, beside the year

explanation.surface: A painter who put the Christian-era dates on his works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A.D.' looks like Anno Domini, but it is the famous monogram of Albrecht Dürer, placed beside the date on his engravings.
explanation.definitionFit: Albrecht Dürer, the Nuremberg artist, signed his works with his initials A and D.

clue.text: East End recess

parts.note: a semicircular recess at the eastern end of a church, behind the altar

explanation.surface: A holiday break in the East End, the working-class district of east London.
explanation.walkthrough: The East End is the inner east London district; here it is the east end of a church, where the domed recess usually sits.
explanation.definitionFit: A vaulted semicircular recess, typically at a church's eastern end beyond the choir.

clue.text: To some degree an essential faculty

definitions.text: To some degree an essential faculty

parts.words: To some degree an essential faculty
parts.note: a university faculty of humanities subjects, whose graduates take a BA degree

explanation.surface: A mental ability that is to an extent indispensable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'faculty' suggests a mental power and 'degree' an extent, but these are university terms: the humanities faculty awarding a Bachelor of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: The humanities faculty at a university awards the BA degree, a core part of most universities.

clue.text: She upset the Dean

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered, so the letters of the name are jumbled

explanation.surface: A woman who annoyed the head of a cathedral or college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' looks like 'annoyed', but it is the anagram signal: DEAN rearranged gives a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl's given name, so it stands for a female, a 'she'.

clue.text: The fabrication of tall stories

parts.note: read literally, this is the construction of a building with many tall storeys

explanation.surface: Someone inventing exaggerated tales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tall stories' looks like exaggerated tales and 'fabrication' like lying, but it is a building being made with high floors (storeys).
explanation.definitionFit: A very tall building is one constructed with many storeys rising high.

clue.text: Short of which, Pobbles are comparatively happy

definitions.text: Short of which, Pobbles are comparatively happy

parts.words: Short of which, Pobbles are comparatively happy
parts.note: Edward Lear's nonsense poem The Pobble Who Has No ... ends with the moral that Pobbles are happier without them

explanation.surface: Imaginary creatures that are happier for lacking something.
explanation.walkthrough: Lear's poem ends: 'Pobbles are happier without their toes'; the 'comparatively' echoes 'happier'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lear's Pobble lost the digits of his feet, and the poem says such creatures are happier without them.

clue.text: . Susceptibility to pain calls for such gentle handling

definitions.meaning: a sore part is tender, sensitive when touched
treating someone with kind softness and care

explanation.surface: A sore spot needs to be handled with care.
explanation.definitionFit: Soreness to the touch is one sense, while loving care and softness of treatment is the other.
